newsitem.title: INDIA: Legacy of India's Rao tainted by legal woes.
newsitem.headline: Legacy of India's Rao tainted by legal woes.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, who launched historic economic reforms, has been dogged by legal woes since suffering a humiliating defeat in general elections this year.
And on Wednesday, he become the first former or serving prime minister of India to appear in court in a criminal case.
Rao weened India's economy from four decades of socialist controls and nurtured closer ties with the United States after assuming power in mid-1991.
But since his Congress party was defeated in elections in April and May, he has been battling for his political life.
He appeared on Wednesday before a local judge to face a criminal indictment in a seven-year-old forgery case.
The former prime minister has not commented publicly on the charges, which carry a maximum penalty of seven years in jail.
He has also been accused of criminal conspiracy to cheat an expatriate businessman of $100,000 in a case that forced him to step down as head of the Congress party in September.
Rao has said he is innocent in the cheating case.
Rao also has been named but not charged in a third case involving alleged vote buying in 1993. He denies any wrongdoing.
Although Congress suffered its worst ever defeat in the polls, Rao, 75, still has a say in the nation's politics.
He remains head of Congress's parliamentary delegation. The party lends crucial support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 13-member, centre-left coalition government.
Rao was plucked from semi-retirement to head the party in 1991 after the assassination of former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi.
He used tact and patience to become the only person outside the Nehru-Gandhi family to complete a full term as prime minister since India gained independence in 1947.
His reticent, often indecisive style irritated rivals and intrigued supporters. Some saw it as the shyness of a backroom man. Others saw the signs of a Machiavelli.
"When I don't take a decision, it's not that I don't think about it," Rao said recently. "I think about it and take a decision not to take a decision."

A widower since 1970 and a man who has undergone major heart surgery, Rao came to power at age 69. Until then he had been content as a backroom scholar, happy among books, writing party documents and the occasional literary piece.
Facing a balance of payments crisis and a large fiscal deficit, he guided India through political upheaval and launched economic reforms that ended decades of socialist controls.
With Rao at the helm, India achieved economic growth of more than six percent in 1994-96. Trade more than doubled and inflation fell to a 10-year low.
In office, Rao quelled a Maoist insurgency in the border state of Assam and successfully oversaw state elections in Punjab, where Sikh militants had fought for independence.
But corruption allegations against Congress leaders, including Rao, multiplied during his tenure and contributed to his party's defeat at the polls.
Seven of Rao's ministers resigned before the elections after being linked to a bribes-for-favours scandal.
